In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.

Tech Report: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.
  • For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope.
  • According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

According to recent reports, the stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a new window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

According to recent reports, freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

It has been revealed that the mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

Sources indicate that these activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

Many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

Sources indicate that the remaining 20 work categories showed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people right now use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

Each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis reveals the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

According to recent reports, by late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Industry observers note that although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

Industry observers note that AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Because freelance projects turn over promptly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a new job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (274 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34152v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.34142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic review systems are increasingly flagging suspected bugs in Linux kernel patches as textual reports. A maintainer who receives such reports needs further inspection to determine whether the report is true. The inspection requires understanding whether the bug can be triggered and, if necessary, manually constructing one. As a consequence, despite the excessive textual explanation, many reports go unanswered. In this paper, we argue that a runnable proof-of-concept (PoC) is the key information in such AI-generated kernel review reports. It is, however, challenging to automatically synthesize a valid and runnable PoC. We present ReproCue, a framework that generates PoCs for AI-generated Linux kernel reviews. ReproCue replays the historical kernel bugs and learns one reproduction finite-state-machine (FSM) per subsystem from successful runs. An FSM records the steps a reproduction goes through, together with the requirements observed at each step. Given a newly introduced review, ReproCue follows the FSM of that subsystem, adjusting the PoC and the environment as execution shows what is missing. In 100 recent AI-generated reviews, ReproCue writes PoCs for 49 of them, compared with 10 for the current agentic reproducer and 9 for the state-of-the-art directed fuzzing. Excitingly, with our generated PoCs, Linux kernel maintainers confirmed 69.4% of them, much higher than 9.3% from Sashiko where only textual explanations are included, making AI reviews more actionable in practice.

arXiv:2611.34130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models are increasingly used in robotics to improve the performance of embodied models. Compared with general-purpose video generation, robotics places more stringent requirements on world models. Generated videos must satisfy fine-grained physical constraints on robot motion and object interactions. However, existing world model benchmarks can overlook robotics specific physical details and struggle to assess them accurately. To address this problem, we introduce WorldPhy, a world model benchmark for accurate, fine-grained evaluation of physical plausibility in robotics. Our benchmark contains 300 tasks, each consisting of an initial-frame image and a task instruction, covering diverse robotics scenes, task categories, viewpoints, and robot configurations. We further collect over 12K high-quality human annotations, and use them to train WorldPhyReward to accurately provide scores and reasons across six fine-grained physical dimensions and an instruction-following dimension. Comparisons with general VLMs and existing reward models show that WorldPhyReward better aligns with human ratings. We system- atically evaluate 13 frontier open and closed-source world models. The results reveal that current world models struggle to consistently maintain fine-grained physical plausibility across different robotics scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuziyuan139/ WorldPhy.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (155 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.34128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate 3D surface reconstruction from unposed images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision. Recent feed-forward pointmap methods eliminate the need for camera poses but inherently produce discrete, sparse representations. In this paper, we present a generalizable pipeline that directly recovers continuous, high-fidelity 3D surfaces from unposed images by seamlessly integrating pointmap- and ray-based representations. Our approach first extracts explicit geometric priors using a pre-trained pointmap model. A query-view-centric selection module then identifies geometrically relevant reference views via a robust surfel voting mechanism. Next, a cross-attention regressor bridges target query rays with reference features to estimate a continuous coarse surface. Lastly, a raylet-based module aggregates local 3D features to carve out high-frequency details and analytical normals. Trained as a single foundation model on 9 diverse datasets, our method demonstrates exceptional zero-shot generalization on 6 unseen datasets, clearly surpassing state-of-the-art baselines in geometric accuracy and detail preservation.

NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies.
  • World foundation models offer a different path.
  • Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

Industry observers note that to improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

According to recent reports, autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Sources indicate that cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Recent findings suggest that model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Industry observers note that cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

Recent findings suggest that while Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

It has been revealed that the immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a upcoming family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

According to recent reports, real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Recent findings suggest that assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

In a recent development, the progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏.

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱.

Sources indicate that looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨.

Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (203 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

Closing the AI guidance gap in education

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drawing on upcoming ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.
  • AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for.
  • Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Drawing on upcoming ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a fresh window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

Industry observers note that this report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:.

Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.

Closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. New research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.

Early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

Recent findings suggest that our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

In a recent development, we are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

It has been revealed that at OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

Recent findings suggest that the choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.34121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.

#40996. Tech Report: GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2647 w)

Tech Report: GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.
  • Industry observers note that the reason is structural.
  • It has been revealed that A bigger fleet still helps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

Industry observers note that the reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

It has been revealed that A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Recent findings suggest that enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

It has been revealed that the same pattern reveals up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

Recent findings suggest that API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

Industry observers note that that shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

Industry observers note that in the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that fresh capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Recent findings suggest that maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

Sources indicate that the discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

Sources indicate that how much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Industry observers note that specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Industry observers note that scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this matter.

Industry observers note that good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

It has been revealed that I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Recent findings suggest that GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy. We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads.

It has been revealed that GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration, allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly.

Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it.

According to recent reports, GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities:.

Industry observers note that scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads.

High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices.

Sources indicate that network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking, while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging, live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics.

Instead of having to manually move workloads to a new cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide:.

Industry observers note that 1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights, and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces.

2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI revision command.

To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run:.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization.

In a recent development, in-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico.

In a recent development, in-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you plan your broader transition.

To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started:.

SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (188 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.34106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.

arXiv:2611.34104v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public admission capacity caps published prior to matriculation are widely used by ministries and institutional analysts as default intake projections in centralized postsecondary clearinghouses. Using an audited 2022 to 2026 Vietnamese undergraduate panel (26,895 program-year records across 309 universities) linked to strictly lagged t-1 occupational vacancy signals, this paper evaluates machine learning, multilevel, and censored econometric estimators against published quotas across 5,385 continuing 2024 programs (five-fold university-grouped cross-validation) and 3,348 matched (2,179 grain-consistent) 2025 programs strictly out of time. Because 62.8% of 2024 programs enroll their exact published quota, unanchored log-growth ensembles degrade accuracy, while the worst 5% generate half of total quota error via unfilled "phantom capacity." Controlled target ablations, including a single-factor test under widened non-binding clipping, show that parameterizing the log fill ratio ln(D_it / S_it) instead of log growth reduces 2024 MAE by 21.5% (14.86 to 11.67), aligns ML with Tobit, Cragg, REML HLM, and capped L1 baselines, and lifts combined tuition and institutional-tier TreeSHAP attribution from 2.5% to 45.8%. Hurdle stacking attains the lowest full-census 2024 MAE (H-Hard 11.29; H-Soft 11.32 vs. 12.35, p = 0.022, clearing 10% not 5% FDR; fold-overlap p = 0.134), whereas continuous QA-Stack outperforms H-Soft on mixed-reporting campuses, Tobit (median) ties H-Soft across both 90% MCS sets, and interior-only Cragg-ML lowers RMSE to 28.1. Under Vietnam's 2025 unified-clearing reform, exact filling falls to 10.4%, H-Soft and capped L1 tie quotas (p = 0.979), and 90% cluster-weighted conformal coverage drops from 89.3% to 74.6%. Across 257 reporting campuses, reconciled 2026 national totals (627,114 to 629,256) lie squarely within 604,533 to 662,044.

AlignPre: Skill-Aligned Post-Training for Latent-Free Generative Precipitation Nowcasting

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (170 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.34101v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precipitation nowcasting requires accurate short-term predictions under rapidly evolving spatiotemporal dynamics. Generative diffusion models can produce detailed and competitive radar forecasts by modeling conditional distributions. However, most existing approaches rely on separately trained components, such as deterministic branches or latent compression modules. More fundamentally, distribution matching alone fails to explicitly optimize operational forecast skill. We propose AlignPre, a streamlined pixel-space nowcasting framework that bridges this gap via skill-aligned post-training (SAPT). AlignPre employs an end-to-end flow-matching forecaster with a hierarchical spatiotemporal architecture for distribution matching and direct radar-field synthesis, without latent compression. During post-training, SAPT exploits the analytic structure of forecast verification scores to construct a differentiable objective. By backpropagating gradients of this objective from radar fields to the generator, SAPT turns forecast verification into direct training feedback. Across three real-world benchmarks spanning different forecast horizons, AlignPre consistently surpasses state-of-the-art deterministic and generative baselines in forecast skill, demonstrating that aligning generative modeling with domain-specific verification provides an effective paradigm for meteorological forecasting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, update on November 19, 2026: Ecommerce and online service businesses based outside the U.S. are now eligible to claim their business and publish agents in ChatGPT.

Originally published on November 10, 2026.

It has been revealed that we’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a latest way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with users via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Sources indicate that together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

In a recent development, in Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, revision key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

It has been revealed that any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.

Business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

We’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share users’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

When a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.

Sources indicate that for customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

Sources indicate that businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent⁠ and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

Recent findings suggest that business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here⁠.

It has been revealed that as people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we initiative to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

Sources indicate that as the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.

Learn more and⁠ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠.

arXiv:2611.34099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34098v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly participate in political discussions, making it important to understand which positions they support or oppose. We propose a framework for assessing LLMs' political stances through simulated social media interactions. The framework uses politicians' posts and multiple prompting methods to identify consistently expressed stances. Using this framework, we construct WorldPOLL, comprising 4,600 political posts from X/Twitter collected from approximately 200 politicians representing ruling and opposition blocs across 23 countries. Our quantitative analysis shows how support and opposition vary across models, countries, and political directions, while our qualitative analysis identifies the political views and policies models support or oppose. Together, these analyses reveal shared positions across models and differences across national contexts. We also examine whether models express consistent stances across prompting methods, investigate the reasons for disagreement, and assess the effects of model size and instruction tuning in stance inconsistency. WorldPOLL offers a practical way to measure LLM political tendencies, identify the views behind them, and assess their consistency in real-world political discussions.

arXiv:2611.34079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating coherent and explorable 3D worlds from scattered images with little or no visual overlap is a fundamental and long-standing challenge in computer vision, which existing geometry-aware methods fail to address. Meanwhile, existing image- and video-based methods may generate unseen regions but produce inconsistent geometry across views. To bridge this gap, we present WorldBridge, a framework for coherent and controllable 3D world generation under scattered images with little or no visual overlap. WorldBridge encodes scattered references into a global scene context to guide geometry and appearance generation across views. Our temporal and spatial reference attention mechanism further enhances the fidelity of temporal references along the target trajectory and supports flexible spatial references outside it. A plug-and-play latent-reference consistency strategy improves reference fidelity through reprojection-guided test-time optimization. We also introduce the WorldBridge benchmark suite to evaluate 3D world generation from scattered, low-overlap references, which is rarely explored by current benchmarks. Both qualitative and quantitative results demonstrate that our method enables controllable and coherent 3D world generation, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art solutions. Our project page is available at https://davidyan2001.github.io/WorldBridge/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s new multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Sources indicate that scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

In a recent development, after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Sources indicate that videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Sources indicate that timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer looks like a really exciting step for practical open-source AI, especially with its focus on local, agentic, and multimodal workloads. A 30B-parameter model combining a 2B vision encoder with a 28B text decoder gives developers a strong foundation for coding, document analysis, personal assistants, and other privacy-sensitive applications. 🔥🤖.

Sources indicate that the Apache 2.0 license is another major highlight because it makes the model much more approachable for developers who want to experiment, customize, and deploy without relying entirely on hosted inference. Local deployment can also bring meaningful benefits around privacy, latency, and infrastructure costs, which makes this especially interesting for personal and enterprise workflows. 🚀.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

In a recent development, the day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.34075v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online services that deploy Image-to-3D models enable customers to generate high-quality 3D assets from a single image. However, the generated 3D geometry can violate content policies and cause broader security risks. To prevent such content, these services typically use policy-restricted inspectors to examine uploaded images before generation. Since the inspector examines only the visible content of the input, a visually benign image can still induce the generation of policy-restricted 3D geometry. However, turning this vulnerability into an effective attack is non-trivial in the black-box setting: global backpropagation through the long DiT generation trajectory is difficult to fit, while different image preprocessing pipelines across services can substantially reduce transferability. In this paper, we present PTA3D, a targeted adversarial attack against Image-to-3D models that addresses these challenges through Prefix Trajectory Alignment (PTA) and Preprocessing Aware Optimization (PAO). PTA progressively aligns the prefix DiT outputs of the adversarial trajectory with those of the target trajectory, where the core geometric structure is formed, allowing the final geometry to be controlled without optimizing through the complete generation trajectory. PAO exposes adversarial optimization to diverse image transformations rather than a single preprocessing pipeline, reducing sensitivity to the mismatch between surrogate and target services. We establish a prefix-to-output bound and a preprocessing-aware transfer bound to theoretically characterize the effectiveness of the two designs. Experiments on three open-source Image-to-3D models and three online services show that PTA3D achieves 41.5%-88.5% ASR on online services and 90.8%-94.6% ASR in white box settings, substantially outperforming existing attacks.
