Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1605 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible.
  • Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.
  • According to recent reports, the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution plans, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

According to recent reports, the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

According to recent reports, we are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

In a recent development, A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

Sources indicate that this is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

In a recent development, each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

For example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:.

Industry observers note that this structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

Running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

@huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:.

Recent findings suggest that the second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

In a recent development, addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

Recent findings suggest that even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

Sources indicate that the version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

Sources indicate that so, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

Across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:.

Some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

We timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

They are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so crucial for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

In a recent development, webGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

With consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

The initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

The pieces reinforce one another:.

Industry observers note that this is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

According to recent reports, the Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the strategy to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

It has been revealed that the area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the newly introduced kernel is wrong, or the test harness had concerns, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

Recent findings suggest that @sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, new-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

Excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Today, we’re releasing a upcoming tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

It is well⁠(opens in a upcoming window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

It has been revealed that we’re building on our current protections with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a upcoming window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

It has been revealed that child safety is an industry-wide issue that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

Recent findings suggest that early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:.

The upcoming classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the new classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

It has been revealed that early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a fresh window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing indicated one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

It has been revealed that more information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a latest window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

According to recent reports, we already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with upcoming product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

Industry observers note that we developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a fresh window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

The protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

According to recent reports, the guidance provides clear rules, ways for users to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our new image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission new guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

In a recent development, protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

It has been revealed that we’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with newly introduced tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

In a recent development, the initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

According to recent reports, these efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.33262v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI models are increasingly being deployed at the edge. Since these models often require significant research and development to produce, are often deployed in potentially hostile environments, and downstream systems often rely on accurate data; protecting them from theft or manipulation is worthy of serious consideration. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), which provide hardware-enforced separation of software execution, can protect model weights but impose strict resource constraints, making full-model execution impractical for large neural networks. We present Onnx2TEE, an automated, model-independent pipeline that partitions ONNX models across rich, trusted execution environments for non-sequential feed-forward networks using graph-aware segmentation to preserve computational dependencies while minimizing boundary communication and reducing TEE-induced inference latency. Evaluation on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin using an Arm TrustZone TEE demonstrates that model parameters can be highly concentrated in individual segments, supporting selective protection of parameter-dense model components. The evaluation further reveals that the generated trusted app's memory requirements depend on both computation and intermediate tensor sizes.

With these APIs, you can check your account balance, find invoices that are due or past due, see which payments and credit memos were applied to each invoice, and confirm that the payment methods on your account are active. You can call the APIs from your own tools or through an AI agent.

Sources indicate that previously, finance teams had to sign in to the console to find past-due invoices, match payments to invoices, or check whether a payment method was still active. Now you can automate these checks with APIs such as GetFinancialRecord, BatchGetFinancialRecord, ListFinancialRecords, GetAccountBalance, GetPaymentInstrument and ListPaymentInstruments. You can integrate the APIs with your accounts payable systems to monitor past-due balances and reconcile AWS invoices on your own schedule.

According to recent reports, the APIs are available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and available to customers in all commercial AWS Regions.

#40880. BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca

BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.
  • Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.
  • Sources indicate that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.

Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a latest method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.

Sources indicate that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following. But the individual tasks inside it may depend on more than that stated goal. Take BBQ, a benchmark designed to test whether models rely on social stereotypes. One question asks about a grandson and grandfather trying to book an Uber. It probes age bias, but also requires the model to track who’s who and reason from the evidence provided rather than assumptions.

And even within a single benchmark, different groups of questions and tasks can measure different things. WildJailbreak, for example, includes harmful jailbreak prompts alongside benign prompts designed to test whether a model refuses harmless requests too often. The harmful prompts are more closely associated with safety, while the benign prompts are more closely associated with general reasoning. Averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference.

BenchMIRT helps researchers separate those signals and see what’s actually driving a benchmark’s score. It does this by analyzing how models perform on each question or task and estimating which underlying capabilities are most closely associated with getting it right.

According to recent reports, benchMIRT takes cues from Item Response Theory (IRT), a technique originating in psychometrics—the field concerned with measuring abilities and traits from patterns of test responses. IRT starts from a simple idea: not every question tells you the same amount about the person taking a test. Some are harder than others, and some do a better job of distinguishing stronger performers from weaker ones.

Researchers have previously applied single-dimensional IRT to individual benchmarks, including in our Fluid Benchmarking work. BenchMIRT extends that approach with multidimensional IRT, or MIRT, allowing it to separate multiple capabilities that may contribute to performance on the same questions.

BenchMIRT applies IRT at both the model and question level. For a given model, it estimates the model’s strength on the capabilities reflected across the selected benchmarks. For each question, it estimates how difficult the question is and how well it distinguishes models that are stronger or weaker on those capabilities.

It has been revealed that we trained BenchMIRT on benchmarking results from 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and more than 34K questions. Six of those benchmarks measure general reasoning, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MATH, and BBH. The other 10 come from our Olmo 3 safety suite, including HarmBench, StrongReject, WildJailbreak, BBQ, WMDP, and XSTest.

Crucially, we didn’t tell BenchMIRT which benchmarks were measuring which capabilities. It independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning. When we repeated our analysis from scratch, those same two dimensions emerged each time, suggesting the result was stable rather than specific to one analysis.

For many benchmarks, BenchMIRT largely confirmed their intended focus: strong performance on reasoning benchmarks tracked with reasoning ability, while strong performance on jailbreak and harmful-content benchmarks tracked with safety.

But BenchMIRT also revealed a more complicated picture in some evaluations.

BBQ, which evaluates social bias and is commonly grouped with safety benchmarks, aligned much more strongly with general reasoning in BenchMIRT’s analysis. That means a low BBQ score may partly reflect difficulty understanding or reasoning through certain questions, rather than safety behavior alone.

Sources indicate that WMDP behaves differently from most safety benchmarks. It tests dangerous dual-use knowledge in areas such as biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity—for example, knowledge that could help someone misuse a biological agent or exploit a computer system. BenchMIRT found that WMDP scores were more strongly associated with general reasoning than with safety. Stronger general reasoning, however, was associated with lower WMDP scores, because the benchmark counts refusing or failing to provide the dangerous knowledge as the desired response.

These findings don’t necessarily mean the benchmarks are flawed or incomplete. Rather, they show that a single benchmark score can combine several different signals—and that BenchMIRT can help disentangle those signals and make the score easier to interpret.

In a recent development, item difficulty and discrimination in both dimensions for Harmbench. Dimension 0 models the safety dimension, while Dimension 1 maps to the general reasoning dimension.

Bar size and direction show the Pearson correlation, across 100 open-weight LLMs, between BenchMIRT ability scores and benchmark scores on a −1 to 1 scale—pink for general reasoning and teal for safety; bars extending left of center are negative. Bold with underline marks each row’s stronger correlation, except where the two are too close to separate; asterisks mark p < 0.01.

BenchMIRT can also help identify which questions in an evaluation are most informative about the capability the benchmark is trying to measure.

Using BenchMIRT’s question-level estimates, we ranked questions across the same 16 benchmarks used to train BenchMIRT and kept those that did the best job of distinguishing stronger from weaker models, while still preserving a mix of easier and harder questions.

Industry observers note that across those benchmarks, keeping only 10% of the questions generally preserved nearly the same picture of which models were stronger or weaker on the underlying safety or reasoning capability as using the full set. Keeping 50% of the questions often matched the full benchmark’s measure of those capabilities even more closely.

BenchMIRT can also use the patterns it learns across models and questions to predict how a model would perform on a benchmark question it hasn’t been observed answering. In our experiments, it correctly predicted whether a model would answer a held-out question correctly 79% of the time. By comparison, a simpler approach that assumes a model will perform on each question about as well as it does on the benchmark overall was correct 70% of the time.

In practice, that means BenchMIRT can estimate model performance more precisely from what it has already learned about the model’s abilities and the demands of each question, without needing to evaluate every model on every question.

BenchMIRT offers a way to better understand and refine the benchmarks researchers use to evaluate model capabilities. By looking at individual questions rather than only overall scores, it can reveal when a benchmark mixes together different capabilities, identify clusters of questions that behave differently from the rest, and surface questions that add little useful information about the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

There are notable limitations. The models we used to train and evaluate BenchMIRT were all released by March 2025, so our analysis doesn’t capture how BenchMIRT behaves on newer generations of LLMs. And the dimensions BenchMIRT discovers depend on the benchmark set it’s given—safety and reasoning emerged as the dominant dimensions across the 16 benchmarks we selected for this project, but a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities.

There are trade-offs, too. If the goal is to rank models by their predicted performance on randomly held-out items, the benchmark’s average score performs slightly better than BenchMIRT. BenchMIRT’s advantage is the finer-grained picture it provides of performance on individual questions.

That question-level detail can also cut both ways: the same estimates that help identify a benchmark’s most informative safety questions could be used to remove them, producing a weaker evaluation that an unsafe model could pass. Existing tools already make it possible to trim evaluations in similar ways, and we think the added transparency into what benchmark questions are actually measuring is worth that risk—but it’s a real one.

Still, we see BenchMIRT – and future tools like it – as a step toward more targeted benchmark design and efficient evaluation. By showing which questions are actually driving a benchmark’s results, these approaches could help researchers build evaluations that are smaller, more focused, and easier to interpret, while giving a clearer picture of the capabilities they’re meant to measure.

It has been revealed that good read! Reliable evaluation is essential for understanding how well AI systems perform and where they need improvement. Benchmarking and systematic testing can help developers make better decisions about model selection, application quality, and readiness for real-world use. In Generative AI app development, these practices are particularly useful for identifying limitations before expanding access or introducing additional features. It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.33257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear attention compresses historical context into a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing the computational and memory costs of long-sequence modeling. From the perspective of test-time regression (TTR), the state matrix can be viewed as an online-learned regression model, where keys and values serve as inputs and targets respectively, and queries are used to read from the model. From this perspective, the effectiveness of state learning depends not only on the update rule but also on how the key-value learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. While existing work has largely focused on how the state is updated and organized, we investigate how the learning pairs used for state updates are constructed. To this end, we propose Sliding-Window Gated DeltaNet (SWGDN), which replaces short convolutions in Delta-Rule linear attention with sliding-window attention to perform content-dependent local aggregation of projected queries, keys, and values. Our experiments show that SWGDN makes the key-value pairs used in consecutive updates more similar in both GDN2 and KDA. In SWGDN, carrying information from the same token across updates can help the recurrent state reinforce a previously learned association. The local mixing strategy can be incorporated into any Delta-Rule-based linear attention architecture without changing its state update equations or chunkwise parallel algorithms. We apply this strategy to two Delta-Rule variants, GDN2 and KDA, and experimental results demonstrate that SWGDN outperforms the original Delta-Rule baseline across multiple benchmarks.

Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a fresh Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions.
  • It has been revealed that “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

The vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Today, we are introducing object enrichments, a fresh Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

It has been revealed that “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal.

Recent findings suggest that to operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:.

Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

Operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems.

Industry observers note that fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

Sources indicate that 1. Reduce costs with Google modelsObject enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience.

2. Generate richer context with GeminiFor complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setupSkip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:.

Recent findings suggest that define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

In a recent development, object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Context lives where the bytes liveInstead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:.

According to recent reports, cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:.

It has been revealed that creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

Industry observers note that automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

Industry observers note that object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources.

Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.
  • In a recent development, the program began as a pilot in July.
  • Recent findings suggest that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science.

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

In a recent development, the program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 newly introduced grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Recent findings suggest that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for latest drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

We’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, fresh research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

In a recent development, we want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

Sources indicate that the program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

Recent findings suggest that the pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for upcoming grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we confirmed when the pilot introduced in July.

We’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Sources indicate that different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and new discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

In a recent development, we’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

Through ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a latest window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

For researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Blueprint⁠ helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

As these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a new window).
